records.name: Jamaica
records.summary:
Jamaica is dangerous for trans visitors. The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books and shapes police culture; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party after being outed — whose killing police failed to investigate, now the subject of an Inter-American Commission case (Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica) documenting state failure to protect trans life.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people remains a live risk — community members report that violence against trans people (beatings, stonings) is common but rarely reported because there is no point. Tourist resorts (Montego Bay, Negril, Ocho Rios) are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare, but a visibly trans visitor outside them faces real outing-violence risk with indifferent police.

sources.claim: Amicus brief (Feb 2024) to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica (murder of a trans teenager), presented by TransWave Jamaica and other Caribbean trans organisations with law-school clinics: documents systemic discrimination against LGBTQ people in Jamaica, with transgender people particularly vulnerable to housing insecurity and educational/employment exclusion.
NOTE: The UNDP report 'Being LGBTI in Jamaica' (Nov 2023) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

Canadian IRB Response to Information Request (Dec 2010) on how Jamaican police treat complaints by LGBT people (2007-2010): NGOs document police harassment - mostly verbal abuse but also physical abuse; the buggery law (up to 10 years with hard labour) and 'gross indecency' between males (up to 2 years) are used to harass men perceived to be gay.

IACHR (OAS) Report on the Situation of Human Rights in Jamaica (Aug 2012): comprehensive official assessment - citizen security, police killings (including May 2010), administration of justice, police impunity, and the situation of LGBT persons.

Human Rights Watch (Nov 2004): letter urging Jamaica's government to protect rights defenders and address violence and abuse based on sexual orientation, after its 'Hated to Death' HIV/homophobia report provoked official denials.

GayToday (2006): Amnesty International's urgent appeal on Jamaica - vigilante violence and police torture; gay men and women 'beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot'; a J-FLAG account of a mob beating a man while chanting 'battyman fi' dead'; Amnesty urged repeal of the criminalising law.

records.name: Jordan
records.summary:
Jordan demands real caution from trans visitors — the safest of the Levantine Arab states by a clear margin, but on a deteriorating trajectory. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 1951, and courts have granted legal gender recognition in individual cases (the 2014 Court of Cassation ruling — though justified by reclassifying the plaintiff as intersex). There is no statute criminalising gender expression itself.

The deterioration is documented: Cairo 52 reports a notable rise in targeting of transgender individuals and spaces by both security forces and civilians, using Ottoman/British-era morality laws; Jordanian security forces coerced queer community spaces into complete cessation of activities; the 2023 cybercrime law (“inciting immorality”) gives authorities a digital tool against LGBT expression; and gender-affirming surgery is criminalised for trans people (Article 8, Medical and Health Liability Law) while permitted for intersex people. In 2021 security forces arrested 14 people at a private party.

For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression per se, but morality-law discretion, shuttered community infrastructure, and family-society hostility make outing dangerous.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 country review of Jordan: notable rise in targeting of trans individuals and spaces by law enforcement and civilians, using Ottoman/British-mandate-era morality laws; new legislation curtails LGBTQ+ speech and digital access; security forces coerced queer community spaces to cease activities, prompting many trans people to leave; legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare are prohibited (intersex people can change markers); medical-liability law penalises professionals providing transition care.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex intimacy decriminalised in 1951; honour killings criminalised 2013; some trans people have changed markers but no clear legal pathway; Article 8 of the 2018 Medical and Health Liability Law criminalises gender-affirming surgery for trans people (allowed for intersex); the 2023 Cybercrime Law criminalises online 'promotion of immorality'; public-decency laws enable arbitrary arrests and event shutdowns.
Human Rights Watch (Jan 2024): 'Jordan: New Threats to Civic Space' — shrinking freedoms of expression and association, affecting LGBT Jordanians among others.

Cairo 52 case digest, Jordanian Court of Cassation Case No 2092/2014 (Oct 2014): granted a young woman's request to amend her documents to reflect her gender change - but justified it by finding she was intersex, not transgender; Jordanian law criminalises sex reassignment (up to 10 years) except for intersex people; the plaintiff had undergone transition procedures overseas for her safety.
Human Rights Watch (Jun 2024): 'Beyond Decriminalization of Same-Sex Relations' — what states must do once sodomy laws are gone, in the regional context of Jordan.

HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - despite state-sponsored repression and stigma, LGBT people are speaking out, building alliances and regional movements; includes an annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across MENA (Jordan among them).

SogiNews (archived RFSL 'LGBT Voices' project, Sida-funded): MENA section of the archived SOGI news site - legacy coverage of sexual-orientation and gender-identity news in the Middle East and North Africa region.
HRW (Dec 2023): 'Jordan: Security Forces Target LGBT Activists' - documents Jordanian security forces' harassment and targeting of LGBT activists, despite Jordan not criminalising same-sex conduct.

records.name: Japan
records.summary:
Japan is a very safe destination for transgender visitors in practice, with a legal framework that lags behind. There is no national anti-discrimination law — the 2023 "understanding" law is symbolic — and legal gender change still requires a court process. But courts have moved in trans people's favour: the Supreme Court struck down the sterilisation requirement for legal gender change in 2023 and ruled workplace bathroom restrictions on a transgender woman illegal the same year.

Day-to-day risk is minimal: violent crime is rare, visibly trans visitors report curiosity more often than hostility, hotels and transport are unproblematic, and Tokyo and Osaka have an established queer scene. The main practical challenge is the strictly gendered, full-nudity culture of hot springs (onsen) — manageable using guides to gender-neutral or private rental baths and mixed open-air baths, which travellers actively share.

One caveat: online transphobic rhetoric and misinformation rose visibly during the 2023 legislative debates, indicating a live culture-war current, though it rarely translates into street-level trouble for visitors.

sources.claim: Official English translation of Japan's Act on the Promotion of Public Understanding of the Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity (Act No. 68 of June 2023): establishes fundamental principles and roles of national/local governments to promote understanding of SOGI diversity - a watered-down 'understanding promotion' law without binding anti-discrimination provisions.

AP (Jul 2023): 'Japan's top court says government restrictions on transgender employee's use of restrooms illegal' — the Supreme Court upholds damages over a ministry's limits on a trans female employee's toilet access.

AP: 'A Japanese court rules it's unconstitutional to require surgery for a change of gender on documents' — landmark ruling in 'Gen Suzuki's' case against the sterilising-surgery requirement for legal gender-marker changes.
Human Rights Watch (Jul 2023): 'Japan Supreme Court Ruling a Victory for Transgender Employees' — the mandatory bathroom-use restriction ruled unlawful.

Kyodo News feature (June 2023): Japan's LGBT understanding law was watered down amid a culture war on transgender issues - activists say the debates entrenched discrimination as much as encouraging openness. (Article later paywalled.)

Japan Cheapo 'All-Gender Hot Spring Guide' (Aug 2024): practical guide for non-binary and trans travellers to Japanese onsen/sento - private and family-room baths, LGBTQ+-friendly onsen, gender-free super sento, and mixed-gender baths; explains the history of bathhouse gender segregation.
Freely travel story: first-person account of what it's like to use onsen in Japan as a trans person - navigating gendered bathhouse culture as a trans traveller.

Japan Gay Guide (updated Aug 2026): 'Is Japan LGBTQ Friendly? What LGBTQ Travelers Can Expect' - physical safety generally very good, same-sex couples usually travel without difficulty, public affection more restrained for all couples; includes related guides on gyms for trans people (IDs, changing rooms).
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404); the underlying Chambers article covered updates on LGBTQ status in Japan and related corporate duties.

GayJapanNews + IGLHRC shadow report to CEDAW (May 2009): 'Discrimination against Lesbians, Bisexual Women and Transgender Persons in Japan' - invisibility, marginalisation and silent prejudice; discrimination in education, employment, housing and healthcare; the Spousal Violence Law and Public Housing Law exclude same-sex couples; calls for anti-discrimination legislation.

records.name: Kazakhstan
records.summary:
Kazakhstan demands real caution from trans visitors — Central Asia's most liveable country for trans people, which is a relative statement. Nothing is criminalised; legal gender recognition exists (heavily medicalised: psychiatric boards, and surgery requirements applied in practice); and revealingly, hundreds of trans people fled TO Kazakhstan from Russia after its propaganda law and LGR ban. ODIHR recorded 62 anti-LGBTI bias incidents in 2024 — real, but documented and reported, which itself indicates functioning civil society (Feminita, ECOM).

The trajectory is the concern: a “We Are Against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda” petition gained official review by the Ministry of Culture in 2024 (HRW urged rejection), and anti-gender MPs are vocal. Currently there is no propaganda statute, no bathroom law, and no police targeting pattern — police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; low visibility keeps visitor exposure small; Almaty/Astana are navigable.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Kazakhstan: hate crimes and police abuse against LGBTQI people continued - an activist nearly run over by a driver who recognised her (no investigation); a trans sex worker harassed, blackmailed and extorted by police posing as clients; hundreds of trans people reportedly came to Kazakhstan from Russia fleeing the war or 'LGBT propaganda' laws; an employment site initially denied an LGBT NGO's registration; anti-LGBTQI statements by politicians, journalists and religious leaders.
OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report for Kazakhstan: no data reported to ODIHR since 2018; no National Point of Contact; civil-society reports for 2024 from ALMA-TQ, ECOM, Feminita and others.
Human Rights Watch (Jul 2024): 'Kazakhstan Should Reject Attempt to Curtail LGBT People's Rights' — the 'LGBT propaganda' bill would further stigmatise and endanger LGBT Kazakhs.

ECOM Regional Report 2024 on violations of the human rights of LGBT people in Eastern Europe and Central Asia (Armenia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Moldova, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Ukraine): documented violations of the right to health, barriers faced by LGBT people, and law-enforcement practices, based on monitoring since 2017.

HRW (Sept 2019): 'Kazakhstan: Supreme Court Upholds Privacy Rights' - the court's ruling protecting privacy rights, significant in the context of proposed 'propaganda' restrictions targeting LGBT content in Kazakhstan.

records.name: Kenya
records.summary:
Kenya is a dangerous destination for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the colonial-era Penal Code (14 years, applies to all including tourists). Police extortion targeting trans people is documented and systemic — a trans woman was forced to pay a $50 bribe in Mombasa, and 25 trans and intersex people told CNN this kind of police harassment is "common." The Kenya Human Rights Commission's "Lives on the Line" report documented 102 evictions, 43 unlawful arrests, and mob violence (groups stripping queer people naked) over a one-year period. An LGBTQ+ activist, Edwin Chiloba, was murdered (his body found in a metal box) — though the perpetrator was sentenced to 50 years, showing enforcement can work.

However, Kenya's courts have been a surprising bright spot. The High Court ruled in 2025 that a trans woman's arrest for "personation" was unconstitutional (awarding damages and ordering the government to draft a Transgender Protection Rights Bill). In May 2026, the High Court affirmed a constitutional right to legal gender recognition. The Supreme Court has upheld LGBTQ+ freedom of association, and the Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional. "Thousands of gay travelers visit annually through specialized tour operators."

There is no anti-discrimination law and no LGR procedure yet, but the court-ordered Transgender Protection Rights Bill is a positive trajectory.

sources.claim: UK Home Office CPIN on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression in Kenya (Feb 2025, updated July 2026): official country-of-origin information and assessment for asylum claims - legal position, societal treatment, state protection.

CNN As Equals investigation: how trans and intersex people survive in Kenya - 'forced to pay bribes at every step'; a young trans woman describes being arrested on a pretext by Mombasa police and held until she paid a $50 bribe; trans people use male pseudonyms for safety; police extortion is systemic.

NOTE: The Kenya Human Rights Commission report 'Lives on the Line: Violence and Discrimination Against Sexual and Gender Minorities in Kenya' (Sept 2025) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

Kenya Human Rights Commission press release (Aug 2025): the High Court in Eldoret affirmed legal recognition of transgender Kenyans and directed the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act, ruling that prisons do not protect trans people's dignity and privacy; the case arose from invasive, nonconsensual medical procedures on a trans woman (SC) during incarceration after a 'personation' arrest.
GATE knowledge-portal article: Kenya's High Court rules there is a constitutional right to legal gender recognition - analysis of the landmark decision.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Dec 2024) covers a Kenyan man sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): progress largely through courts - forced anal testing ruled unconstitutional (2018, compensation awarded 2024); the Supreme Court upheld LGBTQ organisations' freedom to register (2023), followed by pushback including protests and homophobic remarks by religious and political leaders; a 2024 High Court temporary order against incitement to hatred; same-sex conduct remains criminalised and no legal gender recognition.

The Star (Sept 2025): coverage of the KHRC report 'Lives on the Line' - 682 cases of harassment documented across regions (50 sexual harassment, 100 verbal abuse); queer Kenyans face eviction, online trolling, and being waylaid by organised groups who strip and violate them; the country is 'deeply socially conservative'.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Kenya: documents the 2007-08 post-election violence (~1,150 killed), security-force abuses, mob violence, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation under the penal code and societal discrimination.

records.name: Kyrgyzstan
records.summary:
Kyrgyzstan is dangerous for trans visitors — once Central Asia's relative haven, now regressing. In 2023-2024 Kyrgyzstan adopted two discriminatory laws targeting the LGBTI community and restricting LGBTI organisations, accompanied by homophobic/transphobic MP rhetoric; TGEU records Kyrgyzstan (2021) among the countries that removed legal gender recognition entirely (the 2020 Civil Status Acts law blocks birth-certificate changes). Same-sex conduct is legal (1998), but police abuse and extortion of LGBT people are documented, and the community (Kyrgyz Indigo) operates under pressure.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but LGR removal + police extortion culture + active anti-LGBT political campaign make outing risky.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Kyrgyzstan: two discriminatory laws (2023-2024) target the LGBTI community and restrict organisations, amid homophobic political rhetoric; since 2021 trans people cannot obtain legal recognition (Law on Civil Acts amendments); in 2024 Article 47 of the Health Law was amended to bar gender-transition-related medical examination or treatment until age 25 (previously 18); ECOM data show high stigma from law enforcement and healthcare workers, with police abuse of power.

TGEU Trans Rights Index & Map 2024 launch (May 2024): documents polarisation in trans rights across Europe and Central Asia - progress in some countries (Greece, Iceland topping the ranking) and alarming regressions elsewhere, notably Russia's July 2023 ban on medical and legal transition; two new indicators added for 2024.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex activity decriminalised 1998 (equal age of consent 16); 2016 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage; the provision allowing some trans people to change markers was removed in 2020; in early 2026 an MP proposed a bill defining sex as immutable, explicitly banning legal gender recognition and prohibiting any interventions on minors; follows the 2023-2024 'silencing' laws.

ECOM study (2024) on trans people's access to medical services including HIV prevention and HRT across the EECA region (with country coordinators for Georgia, Armenia, Ukraine, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Moldova, Kyrgyzstan, Azerbaijan, Tajikistan) - includes information for trans migrants.

HRW World Report 2020, Kyrgyzstan chapter: includes a Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section - documents the worsening environment for LGBT people, including the 'gay propaganda' bill and violence against women.

RFE/RL (June 2017): 'Curtain Falls On Bishkek's Lone LGBT Club Amid Worsening Atmosphere' - the London club in Bishkek closed; founder Olesya: 'people don't understand what a gay club is... they think we are doing something pornographic. But if they came and saw that it is just a normal club... it would be OK.'

The Guardian (Oct 2017): 'All of us will be victims at some point': why Bishkek's only gay club closed - the Kyrgyz capital was long a liberal beacon in Central Asia until the 'LGBT propaganda' ban; with attacks and rapes on the rise, the community is scared.

records.name: Cambodia
records.summary:
Cambodia is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression — and the government is formally cooperative: it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 Universal Periodic Review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted the UN Independent Expert on SOGI in 2023. Phnom Penh and Siem Reap have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors.

The risks are street-level and police-level rather than legal: the Cambodian Centre for Human Rights documents “shocking” harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported Siem Reap police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse). There is no legal gender recognition yet, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute.

For a visitor: low probability of legal trouble; moderate probability of harassment if visibly trans outside tourist areas; police are a risk factor, not a protection, for trans women especially.

sources.claim: UN Independent Expert on SOGI Victor Madrigal-Borloz's report on his January 2023 visit to Cambodia: assesses implementation of standards on violence and discrimination based on SOGI, gives a panoramic view of the situation of LGBT and gender-diverse Cambodians, identifies good practices and challenges, and makes recommendations.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex activity, but Article 45 of the constitution defines marriage as between one husband and one wife; at its 2024 UPR Cambodia accepted all 12 LGBTIQ recommendations including seven toward marriage equality; no SOGISC discrimination protections; a 2018 two-men wedding ceremony in Kratie was interrupted by authorities.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Phnom Penh Post article covers a study finding abuses prevalent against Cambodia's transgender women.

Rainbow Community Kampuchea (RoCK) page on Cambodia's 4th-cycle UPR: Cambodia officially accepted all 12 SOGIESC/LGBT+ recommendations in 2024 - marriage equality progress, legal gender recognition for self-defined identity, and anti-discrimination measures; includes the civil-society joint submission (Dec 2023) and summary factsheets.

UNDP/USAID 'Being LGBT in Asia: Cambodia Country Report' (2014): participatory review of the legal and social environment - the Civil Code's implicit non-recognition of same-sex marriage, varying police interpretations of laws, Buddhist perceptions of sexuality, and cultural attitudes.
Frommer's travel guide: 'Tips for Gay and Lesbian Travelers' in Cambodia - practical travel advice for LGBT visitors (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

PinkNews (July 2019): RoCK study - 81% of young queer women and trans men in Cambodia suffer emotional abuse by family; violence includes disownment, beatings, forced marriages and forced rehab 'to fix his gender'; 35% of under-35s had considered suicide due to family rejection.

records.name: Kiribati
records.summary: Kiribati is dangerous for trans visitors. Male same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, unenforced); no LGR; tiny, isolated, church-dominated society with no visible community infrastructure.

sources.claim: Erasing 76 Crimes (May 2016): excerpts from the 2015 US State Department Country Reports on LGBTI-focused human rights in seven Pacific countries that still criminalise same-sex intimacy - Kiribati among them.
University of Hawaii Manoa library research guide on Pacific sexual identity - resources on sexual and gender diversity across the Pacific, relevant to Kiribati's cultural context.
Erasing 76 Crimes (Aug 2015): UPR focus on Kuwait and Kiribati - both urged to improve treatment of LGBTI citizens during the 21st UPR session; documents the recommendations each received.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Nov 2016): the UN General Assembly rejected the plan to undo the SOGI Independent Expert mandate (84-77) - notably Kiribati, despite having an anti-homosexuality law, voted to support the LGBTI rapporteur.
